messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 74

# Marcus's Route

Sarah sits in the driver's seat of the number 7 bus, hands gripping the wheel at ten and two, waiting for the light to turn green. She's been driving this route for three years—downtown to the hospital, hospital to the transit center, back again. She knows every pothole, every stop, every regular passenger by name. But her jaw is clenched so tight her dentist has warned her about grinding her teeth at night.

Five years ago, she was twenty. She'd joined the military because her father had, and her grandfather before him. It felt like the natural progression of her life, the way some people go to college. She was stationed in Kandahar for fourteen months, working as a convoy driver—essentially the same job she does now, except the roads were unpredictable and the stakes felt impossibly higher.

The light changes. Sarah accelerates smoothly, her body moving through the familiar motions while her mind splits in two directions at once. Part of her is present: noting the elderly woman boarding at Fifth Street, adjusting her mirror, checking her blind spot. The other part is scanning. Always scanning. The sidewalk ahead. The parked cars. The overpass coming up. Her leg bounces against the floor mat even as she maintains perfect control of the vehicle.

It happened on a Tuesday in March, though she doesn't like to count the exact days anymore. Her convoy was returning from a supply run when an IED detonated beneath the lead vehicle. She wasn't driving that truck—she was third in line—but she was close enough to feel the percussion in her chest, close enough to smell the burning, close enough to see things she still can't fully articulate to anyone, even now.

The worst part, she thinks sometimes, is that nothing visibly changed about her. She came home with all her limbs, all her faculties. Her mother cried with relief at the airport. But something fundamental had reorganized itself in her nervous system, rewired her brain to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that disaster lived in the spaces between one moment and the next.

She passes under the overpass and her shoulders rise toward her ears. She forces them back down. A motorcycle weaves between lanes two cars ahead, and her heart rate spikes so sharply she can taste metal. She grips the wheel tighter, reminds herself that she's on a city street in North America, that the motorcycle is just someone in a hurry, that nothing is happening.

But her body doesn't believe her.

After discharge, she'd tried college for a semester. The lecture halls felt too enclosed, too many exits she couldn't control. She'd tried retail, but the fluorescent lights and constant noise made her feel hunted. Driving the bus seemed logical—she was already trained, already comfortable behind the wheel. Control. Predictability. A defined route.

Except the scanning never stops. The hypervigilance that kept her alive in Kandahar now keeps her exhausted in Seattle. She sleeps maybe four hours a night, waking at 3 a.m. with her heart racing, certain something is wrong. She's stopped going out with friends because crowds feel dangerous. Loud noises—fireworks, backfiring cars, slamming doors—send her into a state of panic she can barely hide from her passengers.

She pulls into the hospital stop and opens the doors. An elderly man boards slowly, and Sarah manages a tight smile. She's good at the smile. She's good at pretending.

As the doors close and she pulls back into traffic, she wonders if this is what the rest of her life looks like: perfectly executed routes, perfect control, and an internal landscape that never stops burning.
